library(rpMMD)

## 1. Introduction

The rpMMD package implements random-projection maximum mean
discrepancy methods for multivariate two-sample testing.

Given two independent samples from distributions P and Q,
the objective is to test

$$
H_0: P = Q \qquad \text{versus} \qquad H_1: P \neq Q.
$$

Random projections reduce the multivariate problem to
a collection of one-dimensional two-sample problems.

## 2. Random projection directions

Independent standard Gaussian vectors are normalized
to generate directions uniformly distributed on the unit sphere.

$$
u_j = \frac{Z_j}{\|Z_j\|_2},
\qquad Z_j \sim N_p(0,I_p).
$$

```{r directions}
set.seed(123)
U <- rpmmd_directions(p = 3, nproj = 5)
U
sqrt(rowSums(U^2))
```

## 3. Projecting multivariate observations

Observations are stored in rows and variables in columns.
Each direction produces a one-dimensional projected sample.

```{r projection}
set.seed(123)
X <- matrix(rnorm(150), nrow = 50, ncol = 3)
Y <- matrix(rnorm(150, mean = 0.5), nrow = 50, ncol = 3)

projected <- rpmmd_project(X, Y, U)

dim(projected$X_proj)
dim(projected$Y_proj)
```

## 4. Gaussian-kernel MMD

The Gaussian kernel with bandwidth h is defined by

$$
k_h(x,y) = \exp\left(-\frac{(x-y)^2}{2h^2}\right).
$$

For a fixed bandwidth, the unbiased squared MMD estimator is

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{MMD}}^2 =
\frac{\sum_{i\neq j}k_h(x_i,x_j)}{n(n-1)}
+
\frac{\sum_{i\neq j}k_h(y_i,y_j)}{m(m-1)}
-
\frac{2\sum_{i,j}k_h(x_i,y_j)}{nm}.
$$

This estimator can take negative values in finite samples.

By default, the bandwidth is selected using the median
of positive pairwise distances in the pooled sample.
This data-dependent choice need not preserve exact
finite-sample unbiasedness.

```{r mmd}
rpmmd_mmd(
  projected$X_proj[, 1],
  projected$Y_proj[, 1]
)
```

## 5. Combined test statistics

Let D_j denote the estimated squared MMD along direction j.
The current implementation uses the following
finite-projection approximations.

### PCvM-type statistic

$$
T_{\mathrm{CvM}} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}D_j.
$$

### PKS-type statistic

$$
T_{\mathrm{KS}} = \sqrt{\max(0,D_1,\ldots,D_K)}.
$$

## 6. Permutation calibration

Under the null hypothesis, independent observations
from the two samples are exchangeable.

Projection directions and pooled bandwidths remain fixed
throughout permutation calibration.

The Monte Carlo permutation p-value is

$$
\widehat p =
\frac{1+\sum_{b=1}^{B}
\mathbf{1}\{T_b \geq T_{\mathrm{obs}}\}}{B+1}.
$$

The implementation includes a small numerical tolerance
when comparing statistics to accommodate rounding errors.

## 7. Example: Mean-shift alternative

```{r cvm-example}
set.seed(456)

fit_cvm <- rpmmd_test(
  X, Y,
  statistic = "cvm",
  nproj = 20,
  nperm = 199
)

print(fit_cvm)
summary(fit_cvm)
```

### Permutation distribution

```{r cvm-plot}
plot(fit_cvm)
```

## 8. PKS example

```{r ks-example}
set.seed(456)

fit_ks <- rpmmd_test(
  X, Y,
  statistic = "ks",
  nproj = 20,
  nperm = 199
)

print(fit_ks)
plot(fit_ks)
```

## 9. Example under the null hypothesis

```{r null-example}
set.seed(789)

X0 <- matrix(rnorm(150), ncol = 3)
Y0 <- matrix(rnorm(150), ncol = 3)

fit_null <- rpmmd_test(
  X0, Y0,
  nproj = 20,
  nperm = 199
)

print(fit_null)
plot(fit_null)
```

A single example does not establish Type I error control.
Systematic simulation studies are planned for later development.

## 10. Computational engines

Both R and C++ implementations are available.
The C++ implementation avoids allocating full kernel matrices
and exploits symmetry in within-sample kernel evaluations.

```{r computational-engines}
set.seed(123)
x <- rnorm(100)
y <- rnorm(120, mean = 0.5)

mmd_r <- rpmmd_mmd(x, y, engine = "r")
mmd_cpp <- rpmmd_mmd(x, y, engine = "cpp")

mmd_r
mmd_cpp
all.equal(mmd_r, mmd_cpp, tolerance = 1e-12)
```

## 11. Remaining development

Future development will include empirical Type I error
and power studies, computational benchmarking,
additional numerical validation, expanded test coverage,
and verification against the motivating paper.

## References

Shi, X., Du, J., and Xie, T. (2025).
